results.question: How many wrong password attempts does it take before smart lockout locks an account in a normal commercial tenant?
results.answer: 10 failed attempts (the default lockout threshold in Azure Public and 21Vianet tenants).
evidence: The default is 10 for Azure Public tenants

results.question: A user got locked out by smart lockout. If they reset their password with 'I forgot my password', do they still have to wait for the lockout to run out?
results.answer: No. Choosing 'I forgot my password' in SSPR resets the lockout duration to 0 seconds. With 'I know my password' the lockout timer keeps running.

results.question: Do passwords of users synced with password hash sync expire in Entra ID?
results.answer: Not by default: for password hash synchronized users the Entra ID password expiration is set to never expire, so they can still sign in to Entra ID with an expired on-premises password unless the cloud password policy is enforced for synced users.
results.evidence: the Microsoft Entra ID password expiration is set to never expire
results.response:
By default, password hash synced users don't expire in Entra ID. By default, for password hash–synchronized users, the Microsoft Entra ID password expiration is set to never expire.[1] Because of this, even after the on-premises AD DS password expires, users can still sign in to Microsoft Entra ID using the expired password.[1]

Where sign-in happens determines which expiration policy applies. When signing in to a domain-joined client device, authentication occurs in on-premises AD DS, so the on-premises AD DS password expiration applies.[1] Sign-ins to the Azure portal or Microsoft 365 are checked against the Entra ID policy.

To make synced users' passwords expire in Entra ID as well, enable the `CloudPasswordPolicyForPasswordSyncedUsersEnabled` feature. Set `$OnPremSync.Features.CloudPasswordPolicyForPasswordSyncedUsersEnabled = $true`, then run Update-MgDirectoryOnPremiseSynchronization with the updated features.[2] Microsoft also recommends matching the expiration period on both sides, since it can become difficult for users to determine when their password will expire[2] if they differ.

results.question: Why does Microsoft recommend blocking legacy authentication protocols?
results.answer: Legacy protocols don't support MFA; more than 97% of credential stuffing attacks and more than 99% of password spray attacks use legacy authentication.
results.evidence: more than 99 percent of password spray attacks
results.response:
Microsoft's main reason is that legacy protocols can't enforce multifactor authentication, which leaves attackers a way around it. Because these protocols lack MFA support, attackers can bypass multifactor authentication requirements by using older protocols[1], and most observed compromising sign-in attempts come from legacy authentication[1].

The scale of the threat is also a factor. Microsoft's analysis found that legacy protocols are used in most of the attacks it sees. Based on Microsoft's analysis more than 97 percent of credential stuffing attacks use legacy authentication and more than 99 percent of password spray attacks use legacy authentication protocols.[2] Microsoft notes that these attacks would stop with basic authentication disabled or blocked.[2]

Legacy authentication covers clients that don't use modern authentication (for example, an Office 2010 client)[1] and any client that uses older mail protocols such as IMAP, SMTP, or POP3[1].

For rollout, Microsoft suggests starting in report-only mode. This policy is put in to Report-only mode to start so administrators can determine the impact they have on existing users.[2]

results.question: What kind of hardware OATH tokens does Entra ID support?
results.answer: OATH TOTP SHA-1 tokens that refresh codes every 30 or 60 seconds; secret keys are limited to 128 characters.
results.evidence: OATH TOTP SHA-1 tokens that refresh codes every 30 or 60 seconds
results.response:
Entra ID supports TOTP-based hardware tokens, not HOTP. OATH time-based one-time password (TOTP) is an open standard that specifies how one-time password (OTP) codes are generated. OATH TOTP can be implemented using either software or hardware to generate the codes. Microsoft Entra ID doesn't support OATH HOTP, a different code generation standard.[1]

Specifically, the service accepts OATH-TOTP SHA-1 and SHA-256 tokens that refresh codes every 30 or 60 seconds[1]. Customers buy these from the vendor of their choice.

Programmable tokens are also supported. Some OATH TOTP hardware tokens are programmable, meaning they don't come with a secret key or seed preprogrammed.[1] Programmable OATH time-based one-time passcode (TOTP) hardware tokens that can be reseeded can also be set up with Microsoft Entra ID in the software token setup flow.[2]

For a helpdesk agent adding a token, note the secret key format: secret keys are limited to 128 characters, which isn't compatible with some tokens. The secret key can only contain the characters *a-z* or *A-Z* and digits *2-7*, and must be encoded in *Base32*.[2]

results.answer: The Backup Authentication Service takes over; resilience defaults are enabled for all policies by default, but it can't evaluate all conditions in real time.
results.evidence: By default, resilience defaults are enabled for all policies
results.response:
During an outage, the Backup Authentication Service handles existing sessions, and Conditional Access policies are applied with limits. If the primary authentication service is unavailable, the Microsoft Entra Backup Authentication Service automatically issues access tokens to applications for existing sessions.[1] The Backup Authentication Service doesn't support new sessions or authentications by guest users.[1]

For existing sessions, policies are reevaluated, but not all conditions can be reevaluated in real time during an outage.[2] Those conditions include group membership, role membership, sign-in risk, user risk, country/region location (resolving new IP or GPS coordinates), and authentication strengths.[2]

Resilience defaults control what happens when a condition can't be checked. Admins can decide whether to block authentications during an outage whenever a policy condition can't be evaluated in real-time, or allow policies to be evaluated using data collected at the beginning of the user's session.[1] Resilience defaults are automatically enabled for all new and existing policies. Microsoft recommends keeping the resilience defaults enabled to reduce the impact of an outage.[3]

Access depends on the session type:
- New session: no access.
- Existing session with no Conditional Access policies: access granted.
- Existing session where required controls such as MFA were previously satisfied: access granted.
- Existing session where required controls weren't previously satisfied: determined by resilience defaults[3].

One caveat for agents: when active, the Backup Authentication Service doesn't evaluate authentication methods required by authentication strengths.[2]

For emergency planning, implement disabled policies that act as secondary resilient access controls in outage or emergency scenarios.[4]

The results don't describe the exact behavior for policies where resilience defaults are disabled beyond denying access when existing sessions expire, so check the full documentation for details.
